other_side: Zitron never engages the skills thesis on its own terms — his piece is a capital-markets argument about whether OpenAI can meet its obligations — but it lands directly underneath it. His claim is that the token-hungry way of working this episode describes is currently being paid for by the vendors rather than the users: the labs sell inference far below cost, and the revenue exists only by "allowing users to burn $14,000 a month in tokens for $200". He points to enterprises moved onto accounts "that required them to pay the actual cost" and then stalling, and to Ramp data showing customers "slow to adopt Anthropic's more-expensive 'Fable' model because of the price". The conclusion is that this demand is shallow and price-elastic — "customers are becoming cost-conscious at exactly the time they need to be spending more" — so the working habits being formed now may not survive being priced properly.
truth_beneath: The single variable both men orbit is the unit cost of running an agent set against the value of the work it displaces. Both accept as fact that inference is currently sold below cost and that usage is climbing very fast. The empirical question that will resolve is what happens when an ordinary knowledge worker's agent habit is priced at cost, and the observable that settles it is renewal behaviour on unsubsidised, metered enterprise contracts — whether seats and token budgets grow once the discounts expire. The residue is pure worldview: Whittemore assumes capability compounds faster than price; Zitron assumes the price is the product. Whittemore is vindicated if unsubsidised agent use keeps growing and something like his five skills turns up in real hiring specs; Zitron if metered accounts flatten and token-maxxing budgets quietly lapse. Both are polemicists with incentives — Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — and the signal is where they agree despite opposite priors: today's token prices are not the real ones. Watch enterprise renewals after the discounts end.
